title: I'm not feeling well
goal: Describe being sick and visit a clinic in Taiwan — while learning to spot verbs that already carry their own object, a pattern that changes how you build sentences.
bekal: name body parts and explain symptoms to a doctor
recognize separable verbs (看病, 吃藥, 睡覺) and insert things in the middle
handle a visit to a Taiwanese clinic and pharmacy

dialogs.title: 對話 — 看醫生
dialogs.intro: Morning in Tainan: Budi wakes up with a sore throat. Xiaomei takes him to the clinic across the street.

notes: ⚠️ **健保卡 (the card for 健保, national health insurance) is one of Taiwan's proudest achievements.** A visit to a 診所 costs only about 150–200 塊, medicine included. **Foreign students who stay longer than six months are entitled to it**, and the premium is about 800 塊 a month.

**診所 (clinic) is different from 醫院 (hospital).** For a cold, a fever, or a minor illness, Taiwanese people go to a 診所 — quick, cheap, no appointment. 醫院 is for serious things. ⚠️ Going to a 醫院 for a cold means waiting for hours and paying more.

**摸摸看 shows the "try it" pattern**: repeated verb + 看 = "do it and see what happens". 試試看 (just try), 吃吃看 (try eating it), 想想看 (think it over). This pattern is very common and makes you sound friendly.
**而已 at the end of a sentence means "that's all, just"**, often reassuring: *感冒而已* ("it's just a cold"), *一百塊而已* ("only a hundred"). It's very Taiwanese and used more often than 只是.
⚠️ **好像 means "seems like, I think"** and is used to soften statements. Taiwanese people use it constantly to avoid sounding too certain — much like "kind of" or "I guess" in English.

grammars.title: Verbs that already carry their object
body: Many Mandarin verbs are really a **verb + noun** stuck together. 吃飯 is literally "eat rice", 睡覺 "sleep a sleep", 看病 "see an illness". Why it matters: you **can't add another object after them**, and modifiers are inserted in the **middle** instead.

Meaning

rows: 睡**了**覺 / 睡**八小時**覺

after: ⚠️ **The classic mistake: 我吃飯麵.** Since 飯 is already the object, you can't add 麵. The right form is **我吃麵** — drop the 飯.

**Quick test:** if a two-syllable verb feels like a general activity with no specific object (eat, sleep, work, swim, sing), it's probably a separable verb. As soon as you have a clear object, drop the second half.
**幫忙 is the most common trap**: *幫忙我* ✗ wrong; *幫我* ✓ or *幫我的忙* ✓.

grammars.title: Describing symptoms: the 哪裡 + 痛 pattern
body: Saying what hurts in Mandarin is very simple: **body part + 痛**. No extra verb, no 是.
after: ⚠️ **痛 and 疼 both mean "hurt"**, but in Taiwan **痛** is far more common. Compare unit 8, where 疼 appears with the meaning "dote on".
**The 了 in 發燒了 and 感冒了 is the marker of change** from unit 11: healthy before, not now. Leaving it out makes the sentence sound like an odd general statement.
**The doctor's first question is always 哪裡不舒服？** — memorize your answer now: body part + 痛, plus how long it's been: *兩天了*.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Notice that many body parts end in **子** or **巴/朵/齒** in the neutral tone: 鼻**子**, 肚**子**, 脖**子**, 嘴**巴**, 耳**朵**. These tails mean nothing — they just make the word two syllables long, because modern Mandarin prefers two-syllable words.

blocks.title: How a Taiwanese clinic works
items: **掛號** (register) at the front desk, handing over your 健保卡 or passport. No appointment; just walk in.
**Wait for your number to be called** — usually ten to thirty minutes at a 診所.
**The doctor examines you for two to five minutes**, then prescribes medicine.
**Pick up the medicine at the window next door**, already sorted into small packets for each dose. ⚠️ You don't need to go to a separate pharmacy.
**Pay at the end**: about 150–200 塊 with 健保, about 800–1,500 塊 without.
⚠️ **藥局 (pharmacies) sell over-the-counter medicine**, but prescription drugs almost always come straight from the clinic.

sections.title: 多 and 少 before a verb

blocks.text: **多** and **少** can stand before a verb to mean "do more…" and "do less…". This form is used all the time to give advice, and it sounds caring, not bossy.

head: 中文

Meaning
rows: don't stay up late so often

blocks.text: ⚠️ **多穿一點 is something you'll hear often from older Taiwanese people**, especially when it's cold. It's a way of caring, not an order — the right reply is *好，謝謝* with a smile, not an explanation that you're not cold.
